summary: S/MIME 3.1 introduced a way to protect email headers end to end, but few implementations used it, and some older ones display or handle such messages badly. This RFC updates S/MIME to define a safer approach to header protection that avoids those rendering and security problems.

eli5.summary: The subject line and other labels on an email can be changed by someone along the way. This gives a safer way to lock them so they can't be quietly altered.

questions: how to protect email subject with s/mime
what is the hp parameter in content-type
subtitle: How to sign and encrypt the Subject and other email header fields, not just the message body, without breaking older mail clients.

tldr.problem: Signed or encrypted email usually protects only the body. An attacker can change the Subject or author without breaking the signature, and the Subject of an encrypted message leaks. The older S/MIME scheme for header protection renders badly in many legacy mail clients.
tldr.mechanism: The header fields are copied into the signed (and, if encrypted, encrypted) payload itself, marked by an hp parameter on its Content-Type. For encrypted mail, a Header Confidentiality Policy decides which outer fields are removed or obscured, and HP-Outer fields record what was left outside. A Legacy Display Element shows hidden fields to old clients.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the RFC 8551 header protection scheme and adds detailed guidance for composing, rendering, replying and forwarding. Mail clients must not generate the old scheme, though they may still read it.

today: RFC 9788 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2025. It updates RFC 8551 by replacing the header protection scheme in that RFC, and no later RFC is listed as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why Headers Need Protection
sections.content:
Most cryptographically protected email today protects only the message Body. That leaves room for attacks: because a signature covers the Body but not the Header Fields, an attacker can swap the Subject or the author without invalidating it. In an encrypted message, an unprotected Subject is visible to anyone watching the message in transit.

S/MIME 3.1 already had a scheme that wrapped a message/rfc822 object inside the cryptographic envelope. The RFC calls it RFC8551HP. Few implementations generate it, and several legacy mail clients (Legacy MUAs) cannot render it. Some cannot show a message/rfc822 subpart at all. Others show it as an attachment, which can strip the security indicators and, for encrypted mail, lead to an unencrypted reply that leaks the content.

This RFC updates RFC 8551 and replaces its scheme. All Header Fields are copied directly into the Cryptographic Payload, with no intervening message/rfc822 object. In an encrypted message, some fields can additionally be made confidential by removing or obscuring them in the outer header section. The design is applicable to PGP/MIME too, although the analysis focuses on S/MIME.

The scope is deliberately narrow: a cleartext message with a single signature, and an encrypted message that contains a single signature. DKIM and DMARC protect headers too, but between mail servers; this scheme works between the mail clients of the sender and the recipient, and also provides confidentiality.
sections.eli5: Normally only the letter inside an envelope is locked up. Someone could scribble a different title on the outside without anyone noticing. This RFC puts the title inside the locked part as well.

sections.title: The New Message Markers
sections.content:
Three small extensions to the Internet Message Format carry the whole scheme.

The hp parameter on the Content-Type at the root of the Cryptographic Payload says the composer intends end-to-end protection of the header fields. Its value is clear (signed, not encrypted) or cipher (signed and encrypted to the recipients). A composer MUST NOT use cipher on an unencrypted message, and MUST use it on any encrypted message with header protection. A renderer MUST NOT treat the presence of hp="cipher" as proof that a layer of encryption is really there.

The hp-legacy-display parameter (only value: 1) goes on a text/plain or text/html leaf part and marks a decorative Legacy Display Element, described below.

The HP-Outer header field appears only in the header section of the Cryptographic Payload of an encrypted message. A composer MUST include one copy, as field-name: value, of every non-structural header field it deliberately left outside the encryption envelope. If a field is present inside but has no matching HP-Outer entry, the composer is asserting that it was made confidential by removal from the outside. HP-Outer fields found anywhere else MUST be ignored.

Only non-structural fields (such as Subject or Keywords) are copied, removed or obscured. Structural fields such as Content-Type and MIME-Version are handled separately.
sections.eli5: Three little stickers do the job. One says the envelope words are locked in. One says a note was added for old mail programs. The third keeps a list of what was left written on the outside.

sections.title: Header Confidentiality Policies
sections.content:
When a message is encrypted, the sender must decide which header fields to hide from mail servers. The RFC calls that decision a Header Confidentiality Policy (HCP): a function hcp(name, val_in) that returns a replacement value, or null to remove the field from the outside. A replacement must be identical, null, or printable 7-bit ASCII. The policy never appears on the wire. Integrity and authenticity need no policy, because they are applied uniformly to every field the composer knows about. Confidentiality is optional because some delivery systems may reject, drop or delay messages whose top-level headers are all removed.

Three policies are registered. hcp_baseline is the recommended default: it replaces the Subject with the fixed string [...] and removes the rarely used Comments and Keywords fields, which should not matter to transport agents. hcp_shy goes further by hiding display names and the time zone in Date, but needs more parsing and is not recommended as a default. hcp_no_confidentiality hides nothing, and a conforming client MUST NOT use it by default.

Every client MUST have a default HCP that protects at least the Subject, and SHOULD NOT make the user choose one. If an HCP changes the From field, the addr-spec SHOULD still match the original, to keep spoofing defenses workable. More ambitious policies, such as removing To and Cc, are allowed but may cause deliverability problems.
sections.eli5: When you mail a locked letter you pick which words on the envelope to cover up. The safe, normal choice is to cover only the title and leave the address so the post office can still deliver it.

sections.title: Rendering a Protected Message
sections.content:
A client that understands header protection changes how it displays mail. It identifies protection by the hp parameter at the root of the Cryptographic Payload (ignored anywhere else). For a field present in the protected section it SHOULD show the protected value and ignore the outer one. For a field present only outside, it SHOULD NOT show it, or else SHOULD mark it as unprotected. It MUST NOT show Legacy Display Elements, and it keeps the original message source available for debugging.

Each header field is given one of four protection states. The state depends on the signature and on whether an exact matching HP-Outer entry exists. A field that was left outside unchanged is only signed-only even in an encrypted message, and it is not private.

Legacy Display Elements are removed before display. For text/plain, the leading lines up to and including the first blank line are discarded. For text/html, a <div> with class header-protection-legacy-display is omitted.

The section also covers messages that cannot be decrypted yet (the Subject may show [...] until the key is available), automated systems that act on email (they MUST rely only on protected header fields and MUST strip Legacy Display Elements before parsing), and RFC8551HP messages, which a client MUST NOT generate but MAY read by inferring the same properties from their structure.
sections.eli5: A modern mail program reads the words from inside the lock, ignores the sticky note meant for old programs, and tells you which parts were really protected.

sections.title: Composing with Legacy Display
sections.content:
A client that composes cryptographically protected mail SHOULD apply header protection, adding hp only at the root of the Cryptographic Payload. Signed-only messages get hp="clear" and all non-structural fields are copied inside. For encrypted messages the composer sets hp="cipher", applies the HCP, writes an HP-Outer field for each field left outside, applies the encryption, and adds the HCP result to the outer header section.

An encrypted message with a hidden Subject would show only [...] in an old client. To help, the composer can add a Legacy Display Element: the removed or obscured user-facing fields, placed in the main body and marked with hp-legacy-display=1. In text/plain they are lines at the start of the content followed by a blank line. In text/html they go in a <div class="header-protection-legacy-display"> that is placed as the first child of <body>, normally with a <pre> element inside.

The element MUST be added only to Main Body Parts, never to attachments, and SHOULD NOT be added to other content types. A composer should unfold folded header values and strip newlines from the element, and in HTML MUST escape <, >, ', " and &. The composer's legacy input is true if any recipient may use a legacy client.
sections.eli5: If the title is hidden, you can also write it on a note at the top of the letter. Old mail programs show the note, and new ones know to hide it because they already have the title.

sections.title: Replying and Forwarding Safely
sections.content:
A client that replies to or forwards an encrypted message must not leak what was confidential. Any header field whose state is encrypted-only or signed-and-encrypted MUST NOT be sent in the clear in the reply or forward. If the Subject was encrypted and gets copied into the reply, the reply's outer Subject must be obscured.

The client SHOULD use the HP-Outer fields of the original to do this. It takes the client's own Respond Function (the code that pre-fills a reply, a reply-all or a forward) and runs it over both the protected fields and the outer fields. The differences yield a one-time HCP that hides the derived fields.

Replies must also go to the right place. When a message has header protection, the replying client MUST fill in the destination fields from the protected fields only. Otherwise an attacker who replays an encrypted message with an extra Cc to themselves in the outer header could receive the cleartext of a reply from a user who knows the attacker's certificate.

Some fields are legitimately added in transit and cannot be protected, such as Received, DKIM-Signature and mailing-list fields like List-Id. A client MAY use these from the outer section.
sections.eli5: When you answer a locked letter, you must not copy the hidden words onto the outside of your answer. And you must send it back to the address written inside the lock, not one someone scribbled outside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The biggest concern is From address spoofing. Mail servers normally check the outer From. A malicious sender could put one address outside and a different one in the protected section, and a naive client would show the protected one. A client SHOULD warn when the outer and inner From addr-specs do not match and there is no valid signature correctly bound to the inner address. In that case a client that depends on its mail server to authenticate the sender SHOULD show the outer From. The RFC walks through each attack case and concludes that the outer field is either the preferred fallback or just as modifiable as the inner one. It notes a risk of a temporary downgrade attack, which the client can end by validating the certificate-to-address binding.

The hp parameter records only the composer's intent. A signed-only message that carries hp="cipher" is still signed-only. If an encryption layer was added in transit and hp is not cipher, the client SHOULD treat every header field as not confidential.

Other risks: Legacy Display Elements must be generated strictly, and protected headers add known and chosen plaintext, so the encryption must be secure against those attacks. The security considerations of RFC 8551, RFC 3156 and RFC 9580 continue to apply to header fields as well as the body.
sections.eli5: A trickster could write one name on the outside of an envelope and another inside. The reader's program has to notice when they do not match and warn you instead of trusting the wrong one.

sections.title: Privacy Limits
sections.content:
Encrypted header fields are not always private. A field copied unchanged to the outside, such as a plain Date, has a copy inside but is not private at all. Even a hidden field is still visible to every intended recipient, so a composing client MUST populate its header list with only information each recipient should have, and be careful with fields such as User-Agent, Message-ID and Bcc.

Hidden fields can also be inferred. If To and Cc are removed, the mailbox the message sits in still hints at a recipient, and encrypted-message structures such as S/MIME RecipientInfo or PGP key IDs point to recipients. Timing can leak through added Received fields or mailbox order, and the domain of From is hard to hide because delivery systems use it for reputation.

A recipient could also overestimate protection. An attacker could remove an outside field that the composer had left in place, making it look like it had been hidden. The HP-Outer match guards against this. For Bcc, the RFC explains that stripping it during encryption may cause a transport agent to drop the message, which is why hcp_baseline does not strip it.
sections.eli5: Hiding words on the envelope does not hide everything. The mail carrier can still guess from the postmark and the mailbox, and the person you wrote to can still read it all.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the HP-Outer header field in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry, with this RFC as the reference and the IETF as change controller. It also added this RFC as a reference for Content-Type, because of the two new parameters.

IANA also created a new Mail Header Confidentiality Policies registry in the MAIL Parameters group, holding the three policies. Only hcp_baseline is marked Recommended. Adding an entry marked N follows Specification Required, while marking one Y, or changing that column, requires IETF Review with the designated expert consulted. A registration needs a stable reference, unambiguous pseudocode, an explanation of how it differs from existing policies and deployment considerations.
sections.eli5: A public list was made so everyone can see the names of the hiding rules and which one is the recommended pick.
